title: How do you answer "Tell me about yourself" in a consulting interview?
description: A structure for "Tell me about yourself" in consulting interviews, a weak and a strong example answer, and what makes the difference.
hook: You answer "Tell me about yourself" with a 60 to 90 second story that has a clear thread: what drives your choices, two quick proof points with results, and why consulting is the natural next step now. It is usually the first question and it sets the tone for everything after. Most candidates either recite their CV or ramble; a short, deliberate story puts you ahead from the first minute.
body:
What the question is testing

The interviewer is not checking your CV, which they have already read. They are asking three things: can you explain yourself clearly and briefly, what are you good at, and does your move into consulting make sense? It is also a chance for you to steer the conversation. Whatever you mention here, they may ask about next, so mention things you want to talk about.

A simple shape

Spoken at a calm pace, 60 to 90 seconds is roughly 150 to 220 words. Split it into three parts:

  1. The thread (about 15 seconds). One line on what has driven your choices. Not "I have always dreamt of consulting", but something true, such as "I like messy problems with numbers behind them".
  2. Two proof points (about 45 seconds). Two moments that show the thread in action, each with a result.
  3. Why now (about 20 seconds). Why consulting is the logical next step, which hands the interviewer a natural next question.

A weak answer

I studied economics at Manchester, then I joined a bank as an analyst, where I did a lot of financial modelling. I also did some volunteering and I like football. Now I'm looking to move into consulting because I like problem solving.

Why it falls short: it is a list of facts with no thread, no evidence of impact and a generic reason for consulting. The interviewer learns nothing the CV did not already tell them.

A strong answer

This example is illustrative; use the shape, not the words.

I've always been drawn to messy problems with numbers behind them. At university I ran the investment society, and when I took over it had about 40 active members. I changed how we ran events, moving from lectures to small live portfolio challenges, and by the end of my year we had 200. After graduating I joined a bank as an analyst. My team's loan approvals were taking too long, so I built a model that flagged which applications needed a full review, and that cut approval time by two days. The part I enjoyed most was presenting it to senior people and getting them to act on it. That's why I'm applying to consulting: I want to do that kind of work across different industries, faster, and directly with clients.

Why it works: it has a thread (messy problems with numbers), two proof points with results, a hint of what the speaker enjoys (persuading senior people) and a "why now" that leads straight into "Why consulting?". It takes about 60 seconds to say.

Make the links do the work

A good answer is not a chronological tour of every job. It is an explanation of what you chose, what you learned and why this role follows. Notice the links in this second illustrative answer, for someone moving from analytics:

I studied engineering because I enjoyed solving unfamiliar problems with data. In my first role I analysed order delays for a retailer and found that a handful of suppliers caused most of the late deliveries. I enjoyed the analysis, but I enjoyed working with procurement to fix it even more. Leading a student volunteering project taught me to persuade people I had no authority over. Both made me want a career that combines analysis with decisions that change how organisations work, which is why I'm applying to consulting.

Engineering led to analysis, analysis exposed a business problem, and fixing it sparked the interest in consulting. Each step explains the next. If you have changed direction, say why in one sentence and move on; a clear reason is more convincing than pretending it was all planned.

Common mistakes

  • Starting at birth or school. Begin where the thread begins, usually university or your first job.
  • Going over two minutes. The interviewer can ask for more. Leave them wanting detail, not waiting for you to finish.
  • No numbers. "Grew the society from 40 to 200 members" sticks; "grew the society" does not.
  • Memorising it word for word. Learn the three parts and the two proof points, then say it slightly differently each time so it sounds like conversation.
  • Inventing drama. Never exaggerate achievements to make the story more impressive. Follow-up questions will find it.

Test your answer

Say it once to a friend, then ask them two questions: what am I good at, and why am I moving into consulting? If they cannot answer both, cut the details that do not help them, and sharpen the thread.

Try it now

1. What is missing from this answer? "I studied history, worked in marketing for three years, and now I want to try consulting."

Show the answer

A thread, proof points and a reason. It needs one line on what drives the speaker, two moments from marketing with results (for example, a campaign they analysed and what changed), and a specific reason consulting is the next step.

2. Write your thread in one sentence. Then name two proof points that support it, each with a number.

Show the answer

A good thread is specific and true ("I like turning messy data into decisions people act on"). Good proof points have a before and after: "cut reporting time from five days to two", "raised $15k for the charity, up from $6k the year before". If you cannot find two proof points, the thread is probably not the right one.

3. Record your full answer and time it.

Show the answer

Aim for 60 to 90 seconds. If you are over, cut background first, never the results or the "why now". Check that your last sentence invites the next question.

Where to practise next

Your answer should lead naturally into the next question, so prepare your "Why consulting?" answer alongside it. The fit interview guide shows how to build the stories behind your proof points, and the list of most common fit questions shows what comes after. To polish delivery, see speaking more clearly.
